index.html.hero.lede: A research-driven media platform exploring African development, knowledge, governance, culture and possibility from an African-centred perspective.

index.html.latest.p: Why African education often prepares young people to leave local opportunities rather than transform them, and what an education designed from African realities would do instead.
index.html.latest.label: >Trained Away: press play
index.html.why.p: Its challenge is that much of its intelligence has not been sufficiently recognised, refined, institutionalised, financed and transformed into collective power. This platform moves beyond describing Africa's problems: it asks how they were produced, what sustains them, what knowledge has been neglected, and what practical alternatives can be built.
index.html.sci.h2: >This is not the past. This is interrupted science.
index.html.sci.p: The clay pot is not a symbol of poverty; it is an off-grid thermodynamic device, refined through generations of empirical experimentation. Using AI speculative imaging, we project what African sciences should look like today, had their development never been violently interrupted.
index.html.sci.cap1: "Subsistence craft": the colonial framing of African knowledge.
index.html.sci.cap2: Thermodynamics, computation, engineering: scientific archives awaiting restoration.
index.html.sci.quote: >What was interrupted can be restored. What was deferred can be recovered.

index.html.theme1.p: How education shapes African identity, ambition, work and possibility.
index.html.theme2.p: How African states can build credible, accountable and culturally grounded systems.
index.html.theme3.p: How inherited knowledge can become contemporary science, enterprise and industry.
index.html.theme4.p: Why Africa imports expertise and how local capability can be strengthened.
index.html.theme5.p: How language, media, religion and global power shape African self-perception.
index.html.theme6.p: How Africans can design cities, institutions, technologies and economies rooted in their realities.
index.html.question.q1: What knowledge did your parents possess that your generation failed to inherit?
index.html.question.q2: What is one thing African education trains us to leave behind?
index.html.question.q3: Can Africa modernise without becoming someone else?
index.html.question.note: Selected responses appear on the site with the contributor's permission.
index.html.voices.p:
Scholars, artisans, students, entrepreneurs, elders, policymakers
      and the diaspora. Each month this platform features one African voice and the knowledge they
      carry. If that is you, or someone you know, tell us.
index.html.written.p:
Articles, research summaries, reading lists and downloadable briefs
      sit alongside the episodes. This is what separates the platform from commentary: every claim
      can be traced to a source.
index.html.join.h2: >Africa's future cannot be imagined by one voice
index.html.join.p: Bring your research, experience, question or story into the conversation.
index.html.founder.alt: alt="Dr Oluwakemi Damola Adejumo-Ayibiowu, wearing an indigo and gold adire-print dress"
index.html.founder.p: Dr Damola is a development economist, Afrocentric scholar, AI generalist, public policy strategist and gospel music artist with over 25 years of experience across government, academia and international consultancy. Through Rethinking Africa she brings scholarship out of restricted academic spaces and into public conversation.
index.html.founder.for: For scholars, students, policymakers, professionals, creators, community leaders, members of the diaspora, and everyone committed to Africa's intellectual and developmental renewal.
index.html.sub.p: Be among the first thousand members of a movement to recover African intelligence and agency. Discover African-centred perspectives grounded in research, watch conversations with scholars and practitioners, and receive new episodes, articles and event invitations, beginning with the free 7 Days of Rethinking series.

quiz.html.quiz.title: <title>The 90-Second Africa Lens Quiz |
quiz.html.quiz.meta.desc: content="Seven questions. Seven things you were never told about African knowledge, and why they stopped. Find out which African future-builder you are."
quiz.html.sub: >How were you taught to see Africa?
quiz.html.lede: Seven questions. After each one, something Africa built, and the reason you never heard about it.
quiz.html.quiz.intro.p: It takes about ninety seconds. You will learn seven things you were probably never taught.
quiz.html.gate.p: We will email you your answers and your full profile. You will also get a short free guide, Seven Things Africa Was Taught to Forget.
quiz.html.gate.name: >Your name</label>
quiz.html.gate.hint: >Your profile appears here once it has been sent to your email.
quiz.html.gate.privacy: We will never share your details. Leave any time.
quiz.html.result.label: >Your African future-builder profile
quiz.html.result.channel: Everything else lives on the channel. New episodes come out regularly, and subscribing is how you get them.
quiz.html.result.motto: Africa must not only be studied. Africa must speak, think, create and determine.

quiz.html.q1: "Growing up, were you taught that knowledge from Europe or America was better than knowledge from Africa?"
quiz.html.q1.a2: "Nobody said it, but I felt it"
quiz.html.q1.a4: "I never thought about it this way"
quiz.html.q1.text: "Six hundred years ago, Timbuktu in Mali was a city of scholars. Families kept libraries in their homes. Hundreds of thousands of handwritten books on medicine, astronomy, mathematics and law. Students came from far away to study there. It was a university city before many European ones existed."
quiz.html.q1.why: "In 1591 an invading army destroyed the scholarly community and its leading scholars were killed or taken away. Later, under French colonial rule, the schools that replaced it taught a different story, and many manuscripts were carried off to Europe. Families hid what was left in boxes and buried them. The books survived. The universities did not."
quiz.html.q2: "Did your education bring you closer to your own community, or take you further away from it?"
quiz.html.q2.text: "Before colonial schooling, most African children learned a trade, a craft or a body of knowledge from the people around them. Farming, weaving, building, healing, trading. Learning happened inside the community and stayed there."
quiz.html.q2.why: "Colonial schools were built for a stated purpose: to produce clerks and messengers who could serve an administration, not builders, inventors or owners. Children were taught in a foreign language, about foreign places, and were punished for speaking their own. When independence came, the flags changed. In many countries the syllabus did not. If school made you feel your home had nothing to teach you, that was the design working, not you failing."
quiz.html.q3: "You see a clay water pot in a village. What do you think?"
quiz.html.q3.a2: "Poverty, honestly. That is what I was taught"
quiz.html.q3.a4: "I use one. I never thought about it"
quiz.html.q3.text: "A clay pot keeps water cold in extreme heat with no electricity at all. Water passes slowly through the clay wall, and as it evaporates on the outside it pulls heat away from the water inside. It is real science, worked out over generations by testing which clay, which thickness, which shape kept water coldest."
quiz.html.q3.why: "Nobody funded it. No laboratory studied it, no company improved it, no patent protected it, no university taught it. It was called craft instead of science, so it stayed the same size for centuries. Today engineers in Europe and the Gulf use exactly this cooling principle in modern buildings, and it is described as an innovation."
quiz.html.q4: "An elder starts explaining traditional knowledge to you. What is your first instinct?"
quiz.html.q4.a2: "Ask how we could test and prove it"
quiz.html.q4.a4: "Introduce them to someone who could use it"
quiz.html.q4.text: "Every computer and phone in the world runs on binary: everything reduced to two states, on or off, 1 or 0, and then combined to build anything. The Ifa system of the Yoruba works on exactly the same principle. Each mark is one of two states. Four marks make one figure. Sixteen figures combine into 256 outcomes, each attached to a body of memorised verses. It is a binary information system, held in trained human memory, over a thousand years old."
quiz.html.q4.why: "It was labelled superstition. Missionaries and colonial officials discouraged it, converts were told to abandon it, and it was never allowed into a single university mathematics department. So the same logic that became the computer in one part of the world was called witchcraft in another. Nobody in Africa was invited to the meeting where binary became a machine."
quiz.html.q5: "What worries you most about Africa today?"
quiz.html.q5.a3: "Identity, and the stories told about us"
quiz.html.q5.text: "Great Zimbabwe is a city of stone walls up to eleven metres high, built without any cement. The stones are cut so precisely that they hold each other in place, and have done for about eight hundred years. It was the centre of a wealthy trading kingdom connected to the Indian Ocean."
quiz.html.q5.why: "When Europeans found it, they refused to believe Africans had built it. Colonial authorities pushed the story that foreigners must have done it. Treasure hunters dug through the site for gold and threw away the very layers of soil that held the proof, destroying the evidence. Later archaeologists who said plainly that Africans built it were pressured to stay quiet. The building was African. So was the truth. Both were buried."
quiz.html.q6: "Do you live in Africa, or outside it?"
quiz.html.q6.text: "The money Africans abroad send home every year is now larger than all the foreign aid the continent receives. It arrives with no conditions, no consultants and no forms. It pays school fees, builds houses, buries parents and starts businesses."
quiz.html.q6.why: "Nothing stopped this one, and that is the point. It is the clearest proof that Africans already fund Africa. What is missing is not money or willingness. It is the institutions that would turn millions of small private acts into schools, factories and companies that outlive the person who paid for them."
quiz.html.q7: "Finish this sentence. Africa's future will be built mainly by..."
quiz.html.q7.text: "Notice the pattern in everything you just read. None of it failed. None of it was disproved. Each one was interrupted: invaded, defunded, renamed, ridiculed or buried. And in every case the knowledge itself survived, in a pot, in a memory, in a wall, in a hidden box."
quiz.html.q7.why: "That is the whole argument of this platform. Africa is not empty of intelligence. Its intelligence was never recognised, protected, funded or passed on properly. That is not a tragedy you inherit. It is unfinished work, and unfinished work can be continued by whoever decides to pick it up."
quiz.html.p.KR.name: "The Knowledge Recoverer"
quiz.html.p.KR.desc: "You feel the loss of what is disappearing. Your instinct is to find it, write it down and keep it, before the last person who remembers is gone."
quiz.html.p.KR.strength: "Your strength is saving memory before it closes."
quiz.html.p.KR.q: "What did your grandparents know that your generation did not learn?"
quiz.html.p.BB.name: "The Bridge Builder"
quiz.html.p.BB.desc: "You live between two worlds, and that is not confusion, it is an advantage. Your instinct is to connect people, money and ideas that would otherwise never meet."
quiz.html.p.BB.strength: "Your strength is standing in two places at once."
quiz.html.p.BB.q: "Who do you know on each side who has never met the other?"
quiz.html.p.SR.name: "The System Reformer"
quiz.html.p.SR.desc: "You know that good intentions are not enough, because systems decide what happens long before individuals do. Your instinct is rules, standards and institutions that work."
quiz.html.p.SR.strength: "Your strength is building what outlasts you."
quiz.html.p.SR.q: "Which broken system near you was designed by someone who never had to live inside it?"
quiz.html.p.ST.name: "The Story Restorer"
quiz.html.p.ST.desc: "You understand that people slowly become the story told about them. Your instinct is words, images and culture that give people back their confidence."
quiz.html.p.ST.strength: "Your strength is changing what people believe they are allowed to want."
quiz.html.p.ST.q: "Whose story about Africa are you still repeating without checking?"
quiz.html.p.FM.name: "The Future Maker"
quiz.html.p.FM.desc: "Recovering the past is not enough for you. You want to build things that have never existed anywhere, starting from African ground."
quiz.html.p.FM.strength: "Your strength is refusing the options you were given."
quiz.html.p.FM.q: "What would you build if you stopped waiting for permission?"

about.html.about.002: >Africa must not only be studied. Africa must speak, think, create and determine.
about.html.about.007: >An African-centred research, media and public-education platform
about.html.about.008: >Rethinking Africa with Dr. Damola explores the ideas, systems and choices shaping Africa's development. Through research-based commentary, documentary storytelling, interviews, public conversations and creative media, the platform examines how Africans understand themselves, educate their children, organise their institutions, preserve their knowledge and imagine their future.
about.html.about.009: >Africa is not empty of intelligence. Its challenge is that much of its intelligence has not been sufficiently recognised, refined, institutionalised, financed and transformed into collective power.
about.html.about.010: >The platform therefore moves beyond simply describing Africa's problems. It asks how those problems were produced, what sustains them, what knowledge has been neglected and what practical alternatives can be built.
about.html.about.011: >The full programme concept note is available for download: Programme Concept Note (PDF).
about.html.about.013: >Africa is frequently presented through the language of crisis, poverty, corruption, dependency and failure. Although these challenges are real, they do not tell the complete African story. Across the continent, valuable knowledge remains hidden in communities, occupations, languages, cultural practices, indigenous institutions and the lived experiences of ordinary people.
about.html.about.014: >At the same time, education and development systems may train Africans to admire what comes from elsewhere while distrusting what emerges from their own environments. Rethinking Africa was created to challenge that intellectual imbalance.
about.html.about.015: >The purpose is not to romanticise the African past or reject knowledge from other parts of the world. It is to strengthen Africa's capacity to engage the world confidently, draw intelligently from global knowledge and participate without surrendering its voice, memory or agency.
about.html.about.017: >Rethinking Africa transforms serious research and lived African experience into accessible public knowledge: research-based video essays, interviews with scholars, practitioners and community knowledge holders, documentaries and field stories, short explainer videos, articles and policy insights, stories of African innovation and enterprise, and intergenerational conversations between elders and young people.
about.html.about.018: >Every story begins with a question. Why does African education sometimes disconnect people from their environments? Why do major African projects continue to depend on imported expertise? Why do young people frequently reject the occupations and knowledge of previous generations? How can indigenous knowledge become modern science, industry and enterprise? How can Africa modernise without becoming a copy of another civilisation?
about.html.about.021: >Africa is treated as a legitimate centre of knowledge, interpretation and possibility.
about.html.about.023: >Arguments are supported by research, data, history, professional experience and community testimony.
about.html.about.025: >The platform confronts colonial legacies, global inequalities and internal African failures without sentimentality.
about.html.about.027: >Criticism must lead towards alternatives, innovation and action.
about.html.about.029: >Complex academic ideas are translated into language everyone can understand.
about.html.about.031: >Not only what happened to Africa, but what Africa can now recover, rebuild and create.
about.html.about.034: >Dr Damola is a development economist, Afrocentric scholar, AI generalist, public policy strategist and gospel music artist with over 25 years of experience spanning government, academia and international consultancy. Her work is driven by purpose, truth and transformation, and it sits at the intersection of policy reform, decolonised knowledge systems, artificial intelligence and creative expression.
about.html.about.035: >As a scholar, her research explores Afrocentric governance, African renaissance and the decolonisation of knowledge. She is a Senior Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of South Africa (UNISA), deepening her work on indigenous knowledge systems, policy innovation and how emerging technologies like AI can reshape Africa's development trajectory when grounded in local realities, asking not just what technology can do, but who it serves and how it aligns with Africa's renaissance agenda.
about.html.about.036: >Her professional journey includes roles in national institutions such as the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Nigerian Revenue Service. Internationally, she has consulted for the World Bank, UNDP, the EU and IFAD on institutional reform, development evaluation and culturally grounded approaches to economic transformation.
about.html.about.037: >She has published and presented across Africa, Europe and North America, and holds a PhD in Development Studies (UNISA), an MSc in Poverty Reduction and Development Management (University of Birmingham, UK) and a BSc in Economics (Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria). She is a Prosci® Certified Change Management Practitioner and a member of AIKRN, CITN, NIM, ANAN and NES.
about.html.about.038: >Beyond academia and policy, she is a songwriter and founder of the Oratorio Music Foundation (est. 1996), through which she has mentored young people and led campus-based gospel music initiatives. As the daughter of the legendary Nigerian comedian Baba Sala, she carries forward a family legacy of creative impact through music and comedy released under the name Oyindamola.
about.html.about.039: >Across all she does, Dr Damola seeks to advance Africa-centred scholarship and AI applications that challenge dominant paradigms; reform public sector systems for equity, accountability and national growth; nurture Afrocentric leadership that fuses wisdom, technology and cultural values; and use music and mentorship to draw hearts back to God and inspire transformation.
about.html.about.041: >Not a platform where one person speaks
about.html.about.042: >Rethinking Africa is a growing community of scholars, students, professionals, artists, entrepreneurs, policymakers, artisans, elders, young people and members of the African diaspora.
about.html.about.043: >You are invited to propose a story or episode, participate in an interview, contribute a research reflection, recommend a scholar or practitioner, share a community innovation, identify neglected African knowledge, suggest solutions to development challenges, or partner on research, media and public-engagement projects.

ideas.html.ideas.007: >The written spine of the programme. This is what distinguishes it from opinion-based channels.
ideas.html.ideas.009: >From Clay Pots to Quantum Futures: Rethinking African Science, Innovation, and Global Belonging
ideas.html.ideas.011: >African knowledge was not pre-scientific; it was scientific, empirical, experimental and adaptive. What disrupted it was violent interruption, not internal failure. This paper uses speculative design and AI imaging to project indigenous sciences (the clay pot's thermodynamics, Ifá's binary combinatorics, Great Zimbabwe's engineering, Aroko's semiotic networks) into quantum-era futures, and proposes six epistemic principles of African scientific reasoning.

policies.html.policies.001: <title>Privacy, Terms and Copyright | Rethinking Africa with Dr. Damola</title>
policies.html.policies.002: content="Privacy policy, terms of use, copyright and consent information."
policies.html.policies.006: >How this platform protects visitors, contributors and its own work.
policies.html.policies.008: >We collect only what the subscription and contribution forms request (name, email, country and area of interest) and use it solely to send the newsletter, respond to submissions and improve the programme. We do not sell or share personal data. You may unsubscribe or request deletion at any time by writing to drdamolaafrica@gmail.com.
policies.html.policies.010: >Content is provided for public education. Visitors may share and quote materials with attribution and a link. Submitting a contribution grants the programme permission to review it; nothing is published without the contributor's consent.
policies.html.policies.012: >© Rethinking Africa with Dr. Damola. Episodes, articles, graphics and the programme identity are protected. Guests and contributors retain rights over their own words and images; interview and photograph consent is obtained before publication, and any participant may request corrections or removal of their contribution.

editorial.html.editorial.001: <title>Editorial Standards | Rethinking Africa with Dr. Damola</title>
editorial.html.editorial.002: content="How Rethinking Africa verifies research, selects sources, handles corrections and protects contributors."
editorial.html.editorial.006: >The platform sits between scholarship, journalism, documentary and public education. These standards keep it trustworthy.
editorial.html.editorial.009: >Claims are supported by credible research, historical records, data, field observation or community testimony before publication.
editorial.html.editorial.011: >We favour primary sources, peer-reviewed work and named expertise, and clearly distinguish facts from interpretation and speculation.
editorial.html.editorial.013: >Verified errors are corrected promptly and visibly on the relevant page or episode description. Corrections may be requested at drdamolaafrica@gmail.com.
editorial.html.editorial.015: >Guests are quoted in context, informed of how material will be used, and may review their approved photographs and quotations.
editorial.html.editorial.017: >Where artificial intelligence, reenactment or dramatisation is used, it is disclosed in the content itself.
editorial.html.editorial.019: >Submitted stories are handled confidentially; nothing is published without consent, and identities are protected on request.
editorial.html.editorial.021: >Major episodes carry their references and reading lists on the Ideas page, so viewers, students and researchers can verify sources and go deeper.
